description: We are SpaceNuts, a team of six young innovators from Panama passionate about technology, creativity, and problem-solving. With skills in software development, engineering, design, research, and communication, we created 2Mars as an interactive learning experience. We see competitions as opportunities to grow, collaborate, share ideas, and inspire innovation. We believe technology has the power to solve real-world challenges and create a better future.
summary:
We developed 2Mars, an interactive Mars mission design game that puts players in the role of a space mission team. The game transforms the complexity of interplanetary exploration into a hands-on experience where players must plan, design, and manage a mission to Mars.
Players make engineering decisions involving destination and landing site selection, launch vehicle capabilities, spacecraft mass, launch windows, trajectories, rover configuration, and resource management. Each choice introduces trade-offs that shape the mission: a heavier rover affects mission requirements, while scientific instruments compete for limited power and space, influencing what the mission can investigate.
Beyond mission design, players experience the consequences of their decisions through the mission's progression, from planning and launch to landing and scientific exploration. Local two-player cooperative gameplay, distinct mission roles, bilingual support, and Dr. Owen, the in-game mission guide, make the experience collaborative and accessible.
2Mars addresses NASA's challenge by connecting the engineering decisions behind a space mission with the challenges of carrying it out, allowing players to explore how technical constraints and scientific objectives shape a mission's success.
details:
How It Works

2Mars is an interactive Mars mission design and management game developed in Godot Engine 4.7. It puts players in the roles of a mission team, allowing them to experience the challenges of planning, carrying out, and evaluating a robotic expedition to Mars.

Players begin by defining mission objectives and making engineering decisions that shape their expedition. They evaluate launch vehicle capabilities, spacecraft mass, launch windows and trajectories, select a destination and landing site, configure a rover, and consider the resources required to complete their objectives. These decisions connect mission planning with the challenges that follow.

Once the mission begins, players experience key stages of a robotic Mars expedition, including launch, interplanetary transit, the landing sequence known as the Seven Minutes of Terror, and surface operations. On Mars, they explore different environments, investigate scientific targets, manage rover resources, and collect samples to accomplish their mission objectives.

The game features Campaign and Sandbox modes, four Martian exploration zones, approximately 30 rover component options, and seven scientific instruments. It also includes local two-player cooperative gameplay, in which participants divide responsibilities between the Mission Commander and Rover Engineer & Scientist roles. A bilingual interface and Dr. Owen, an interactive mission guide, provide context and help players understand the purpose and consequences of their decisions.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Designing a space mission involves complex scientific and engineering concepts that are often difficult to understand without specialized knowledge or access to professional tools. For students and people interested in space exploration, the relationships between mission objectives, spacecraft design, resources, and scientific outcomes can remain abstract.

2Mars addresses this accessibility barrier by turning those concepts into decisions players can experience. Instead of only reading about mission engineering, players apply concepts, manage constraints, face challenges, and observe how their choices influence the mission.

Its intended impact is to make planetary exploration more approachable and encourage interest in STEM fields, particularly aerospace engineering, robotics, and planetary science. The cooperative mode also creates opportunities for communication, shared problem-solving, and teamwork.

The game has undergone manual internal playtesting: team members played complete game sessions to assess the experience from mission planning through surface operations. These tests helped the team review gameplay flow, mission progression, functionality, and the connection between decisions and outcomes. Its educational impact, however, has not yet been formally measured through studies with external students or educators.

Creativity and Innovation

The central creative approach of 2Mars is to connect mission design, engineering decisions, and scientific exploration within one continuous gameplay experience. Rather than presenting spacecraft design and planetary exploration as separate activities, the game links them: the rover and mission decisions made during planning shape the possibilities and challenges players encounter later.

The cooperative mode adds a complementary dimension by assigning different responsibilities to two players. Mission success requires coordination between the Mission Commander and Rover Engineer & Scientist, making collaboration part of the problem-solving process rather than simply allowing both players to perform the same tasks.

Campaign and Sandbox modes offer different ways to engage with the experience: players can follow structured mission objectives or experiment with configurations and strategies. The exploration zones, rover components, scientific instruments, and Dr. Owen's guidance further connect interactive gameplay with the complexity of robotic exploration.

This combination transforms a technically complex process into an experience where players can understand not only what a mission does, but why engineering choices matter.

Tools and Technologies

2Mars was developed using Godot Engine 4.7 and GDScript, which power its gameplay systems, mission logic, interfaces, and interactive mechanics.

The development workflow combined programming tools, AI-assisted development, creative software, and project management platforms:

  • Godot Engine 4.7 and GDScript: Core game engine and programming language used to develop the game.
  • Claude (Fable) and OpenAI Codex (Astra): Assisted with programming, implementation, debugging, and iterative development.
  • Claude: Generated in-game visual assets based on art direction, style references, and typography guidelines prepared by the team in Canva.
  • ChatGPT: Generated the SpaceNuts team logo and 2Mars project logo, and assisted with organizing project information and preparing and structuring documentation for the GitHub repository.
  • Higgsfield: Generated animations incorporated into the game, including the launch sequence and additional rover animations.
  • Microsoft Copilot: Helped consolidate information from multiple Excel spreadsheets into a unified workbook for organizing rover components, engineering trade-offs, and technical references.
  • Canva: Used to create visual references and establish the game's art direction, typography, and design guidelines.
  • GitHub: Used for version control, collaboration, and project documentation.
  • Vercel: Used to deploy and host the web-exported Godot game, making it accessible through a browser.

The project was designed as a software-based experience and does not require dedicated physical hardware to play. Its browser deployment makes it accessible through compatible computers without requiring players to install the Godot development environment.

Factors Considered

Throughout development, the team balanced five considerations: scientific credibility, ensuring that the experience remained grounded in real planetary exploration; engineering relationships, connecting design decisions to operational consequences; accessibility, through bilingual content and interactive guidance; technical feasibility, working within the capabilities of the chosen engine and browser deployment; and gameplay and collaboration, balancing the experience while giving cooperative players distinct responsibilities.

Scientific Foundation

Scientific credibility was a key consideration throughout 2Mars's development. The team researched NASA and JPL mission documentation, particularly the Mars 2020 mission and Perseverance rover, to inform the game's scientific objectives, engineering systems, and exploration mechanics. This research influenced not only the information presented in the game, but also how the team approached its design. Three examples illustrate how real mission discoveries shaped its mechanics:

  • Communications — From a single link to communication constraints. The team's initial model treated data return as a single direct-to-Earth connection. NASA research revealed two distinct communication paths: UHF relay through orbiters, reaching up to 2 Mbps during communication windows, and direct X-band transmission, whose rates depend on ground antenna capabilities. This changed the mission model to include relay opportunities, onboard data storage, and decisions about when to transmit observations. In-game transmission speeds are accelerated for playability, with NASA reference values distinguished from game parameters. (NASA Glenn · NASA Rover Components)
  • Mobility — Connecting terrain to rover durability. Research into Curiosity's wheel damage and Perseverance's redesigned wheels revealed how terrain conditions influence rover engineering. Perseverance uses 48 gently curved treads and a thicker wheel skin compared with Curiosity's 24 chevron treads. This research informed 2Mars's terrain-related wheel wear and durability choices, making mobility a mission-planning consideration. Wear rates and component upgrades remain simplified gameplay mechanics. (NASA/JPL)
  • Sampling — Learning from an unsuccessful experiment. Perseverance's first sampling attempt at the Roubion rock produced an empty tube after the material crumbled during drilling. This challenged the assumption that reaching a scientific target guarantees a successful sample. 2Mars translates this uncertainty into fragile-rock scenarios where players inspect targets and decide whether to retry or investigate alternative material. Failed attempts introduce gameplay costs in time and energy. (NASA Science)

NASA's four Perseverance science objectives also inform the themes of the game's four exploration zones, while documentation of its seven scientific instruments provides a reference for equipment functions and compatibility requirements. These connections help give scientific exploration a purpose beyond simply visiting different Martian environments.

The research is documented in the team's GitHub repository and complemented by an in-game Science Resources section, connecting references to concepts such as rover mobility, wheel wear, energy systems, communications, geological investigation, scientific instruments, and sample collection.

The game distinguishes verified mission information from science-informed abstractions and fictional elements. Component specifications, resource capacities, wear rates, transmission speeds, and other parameters may be simplified for gameplay balance. 2Mars uses publicly available NASA mission documentation, not live telemetry or raw spacecraft datasets.
